title: Tablet and e-reader: safe teardown
summary: A dead tablet or e-reader gives a large lithium pouch pack, cover magnets, small speakers and, from LCD models, a backlight strip with light-spreading sheets. The battery is glued to the case: work it free with gentle heat or isopropyl alcohol and flat plastic cards, never by prying or bending the cells, which can catch fire.

steps.text: Check it first, before you charge it. Look along every edge and feel the back with the back of your hand. If the screen is lifting, the back bulges, or the tablet is hot or smells sweet, the battery is failing: stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium instead of this guide. If it looks normal, charge it on concrete, stone or a metal tray where you can watch it, and unplug it at once if it gets warm. Then switch it on: a working tablet or e-reader is a library, so load it with manuals and reference books instead.
steps.warn: Never charge, heat or press on a swollen tablet.

steps.text: Set up outdoors, or on concrete, stone or a metal tray, away from anything that burns, with a bucket of dry sand and a metal tin close by. You need small screwdrivers and Torx bits, plastic opening picks, three or four old plastic cards, a suction cup, a hair dryer, safety glasses, packing tape and isopropyl alcohol of 90% or stronger.
steps.warn: Isopropyl alcohol is flammable. No flames, smoking or sparks while it is open.

steps.text: If it still runs, use it until the battery is below about 25%, then switch it off fully. Take out any SIM tray or memory card and take off any cover.

Find the way in. Many e-readers and budget tablets have a plastic back or a front bezel held by clips: work a plastic pick round the seam to pop the clips, then undo the small Torx screws inside, and go to the battery connector step. iPads and most thin tablets have the screen glued to the case: do the next step.

Glued screens: cover cracked glass with packing tape. Set the hair dryer on low and warm one edge until it is warm, not hot: you must be able to keep your hand on the case. Keep it under about 54 °C (130 °F). Press the suction cup near that edge, lift gently, and slide the tip of a pick into the gap. Work round the edge with several picks, warming again as it cools. Never push a pick in more than 6 mm (1/4 in), and less near cameras and buttons: the battery fills most of the back.
steps.warn: Heat above about 54 °C (130 °F) can damage the battery and set it off: no flame, no heat gun. The glass flexes and cracks: wear glasses. Never heat a swollen tablet.

steps.text: Lift the screen slowly to see where its cables run, and don't stretch them. Now look at the battery. If it is puffed, its wrapper is wrinkled or wet, or you smell something sweet, stop: do not heat, pry or charge it, and follow safety_swollen_lithium. Then disconnect the battery: undo the cover over its connector and lift the connector up with a plastic pick. On iPads with screwed battery contacts, take out that screw and slide a thin plastic card between the contacts.
steps.warn: Metal tools near the battery contacts can short the battery. Use plastic.

steps.text: Unplug the screen's ribbon cables and lift the screen away. Keep it flat in a box if you have another tablet of the same model; otherwise see the backlight step.

Loosen the battery glue. Tablet packs are big and often two cells side by side. Run 1–2 drops of isopropyl alcohol under each edge and wait a few minutes. Don't use the hair dryer while the alcohol is wet. If the glue holds, let the alcohol dry, then warm the outside of the case under the battery with the hair dryer on low, under about 54 °C (130 °F), and wait again.

Slide plastic cards under the battery from a long edge, keeping them flat, and work them slowly across to cut the glue. Leave each card in place and add the next. Lift the pack only when it is loose everywhere. Watch for ribbon cables under the cards.
steps.warn: If the pack starts to bend, stop and wait. Add a drop of alcohol, or once the alcohol has dried warm the case gently, under about 54 °C (130 °F). Never lever, poke or pry the battery with any metal tool. Bending or puncturing it can start a fire.

steps.text: Lay the battery on dry sand in the tin and tape over its connector or contacts. Until you test it, cover it with sand, put the lid on loosely and keep the tin outdoors or in an empty shed, away from where people sleep. Let any alcohol dry for at least 10 minutes before you charge, solder or warm it. Check it as in the notes.
steps.warn: A pack that gets hot, hisses or swells goes outdoors into sand now. See safety_swollen_lithium.

steps.text: Take out the speakers, usually at the short edges. Undo their screws, unplug or unclip their contacts and lift them out.

Collect the magnets: small bars along the edges inside the case on models made for magnetic covers. Ease them out with a plastic tool and keep each magnet apart, with a card between, so they can't snap together.
steps.warn: Keep magnets away from pacemakers. Two small magnets swallowed by a child can pull together through the gut.

steps.text: On an LCD screen that is beyond repair, you can try for the backlight (panel layouts vary and none of the cited teardowns shows this step). Peel the tape or thin metal frame off the back of the panel, lift the glass layer away, then take out the thin plastic sheets, the clear light-guide plate and the LED strip along one edge.
steps.warn: LCD glass is thin and breaks into sharp slivers. Wear gloves and glasses, and work over a tray.

steps.text: Unclip the camera modules and bag them with the logic board as spares for the same model. The board still holds the owner's files.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The whole tablet or e-reader, if it works.** An e-reader runs for weeks on one charge and holds thousands of books. Strip only ones that are dead or past repair.
- **Battery.** A 3.7 V lithium polymer pack: 890 mAh (3.29 Wh) in a Kindle 7th generation (iFixit Kindle 7th Gen), 3,400 mAh (12.6 Wh) in a Fire HD 6 (iFixit Fire HD 6) and 27.3 Wh in an iPad Air 2 (Apple iPad Air 2 specs), which is two cells in one pack (iFixit iPad Air 2 battery). Keep the cells joined, and keep the protection board on if the pack has one (check yours; no cited source shows one in every tablet pack). A pack with a protection board and a 3.7 V label can run LED lights and radios through a single-cell USB charge board from a power bank (teardown_power_bank). Use the pack's own plug if it fits. If you must solder, solder only to the protection board's pads, never to the cell's foil tabs, keep each joint to a few seconds so the heat doesn't reach the cells, and stop if the pack feels warm. Charge it only on sand or metal where you can watch it, and unplug it if it warms up.
- **Magnets.** Tablets made for magnetic covers carry small magnets along their edges, probably neodymium. On the iPad Air 2 the Smart Cover magnets are the only parts left in the empty rear case (iFixit iPad Air 2). Use them for catches, tool holders and picking small screws out of dirt.
- **Speakers.** Small sealed speaker boxes for radios, alarms and intercoms.
- **Backlight parts (LCD models).** LCD tablets are lit from behind by LEDs (the iPad Air 2's screen is an LED-backlit IPS panel; Apple iPad Air 2 specs). Behind the LCD sit a strip of small LEDs, a clear light-guide plate and thin diffuser sheets. The plate and sheets spread LED light into an even glow: good covers for home-made LED lamps (build_led_lighting_12v). E-ink screens have no LCD backlight; some e-readers have a thin front light of their own instead, so check yours.
- **Cameras and screen.** Spares for the same model only.

## Getting the battery out without a fire

- Run the battery below about 25% first; iFixit advises this for phones to cut the risk of a dangerous thermal event (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery), and tablet packs hold more energy.
- iFixit softens iPad adhesive with a microwaved heating pad (the iOpener), heated 30 seconds at a time until barely too hot to touch and never above 100 °C; those limits are for the pad, not for the tablet (iFixit iPad Air 2 battery). Keep the tablet itself cooler: OSHA lists heat above about 54 °C (130 °F) as able to damage lithium batteries (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019).
- Slide plastic cards under the battery and keep them flat. Bending the battery can damage it and release dangerous chemicals; if it starts to bend, iFixit reheats and starts again (iFixit iPad Air 2 battery).
- Avoid metal tools except on screws, so you don't short the battery (iFixit iPad Air 2 battery).
- On the Fire HD 6 iFixit needed excessive force even with a plastic card and called the adhesive a hazard (iFixit Fire HD 6); the Kindle 7th generation's battery glue is also much stronger than it needs to be (iFixit Kindle 7th Gen). Let isopropyl alcohol of over 90% soften it instead of forcing it (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery); it is flammable, so use it sparingly and keep heat away until it has dried (iFixit swollen battery).
- For a swollen pack: no heat, plastic tools only, and solvent instead of prying (iFixit swollen battery; iFixit Galaxy S10e battery). Then follow safety_swollen_lithium.

## Variations

- **Fire HD 6:** the plastic back is held by clips with no adhesive and opens with a pick; the screws inside are all T5 Torx; the battery is glued in hard (iFixit Fire HD 6).
- **Kindle 7th generation (basic e-reader):** the front bezel is held by mild adhesive and clips and needs no heat; T5 Torx screws; the battery and board sit on the display's midframe; the touch sensing is an infrared grid on two boards along the screen edges (iFixit Kindle 7th Gen).
- **iPad Air 2:** no outside screws; heat softens the screen adhesive; the glass and LCD are fused, so a cracked screen means the whole assembly; the two-cell battery is glued to the case; iFixit rated it 2 out of 10 for repair (iFixit iPad Air 2). iFixit keeps picks no more than 6 mm (1/4 in) in, and less near the home button (iFixit iPad Air 2 battery).

## What to leave

- **The logic board.** Almost nothing on it can be reused by hand. Keep it whole as a spare or for the owner's files.
- **An e-ink panel.** It needs its own controller board to show anything.
- **Fused glass and LCD from a cracked iPad,** unless you want the backlight sheets: it breaks into slivers as you separate it.
- **Any pack that bent, dented, swelled, leaked or rests below 2.0 V.** Tape its contacts and store it in sand (safety_swollen_lithium). Don't put lithium batteries in household rubbish or recycling bins (EPA lithium-ion batteries).

## Testing what you got out

- **Battery.** If you can reach the protection board's output pads, measure DC volts. Above 3.0 V: probably fine. 2.5–3.0 V: fine to charge. 2.0–2.5 V: suspect. Below 2.0 V: reject, and never charge it. To charge, use a charger that stops at 4.2 V, set the pack on a metal tray of sand where you can watch it, and feel it every 15 minutes: if it gets hot or swells, unplug it and retire it to the sand (safety_swollen_lithium). Then follow test_lithium_cell.
- **Speaker.** Touch a 1.5 V cell across its contacts for a moment. A click means the coil is whole.
- **LED strip.** Backlight strips are often several LEDs in series and need more than one cell's voltage. Try it from 9–12 V through a 1 kΩ resistor, as in teardown_led_bulb. If it stays dark, the string may need more volts than you have; never connect it straight to a battery.
